profile.name: Valse à deux temps
profile.tagline: A 19th-century Russian-origin waltz featuring two steps per three-beat measure.
profile.insight: In 1839, the Baron de Nieuken introduced the Valse à deux temps to Paris, where he performed two steps over a three-beat measure, causing the traditional three-beat waltz to fall out of favor in elite salons.
profile.profile: The Valse à deux temps is a 19th-century ballroom dance that originated in Russia and gained popularity in Parisian high society after 1839. Unlike the traditional three-beat waltz, this style compresses two steps into a single three-beat measure, creating a distinct rhythmic tension. It relies on a slide and a quick follow-up step, performed with a slight knee bend. The dance was initially adopted by the Russian delegation in Paris before spreading to public ballrooms like La Chaumière.
profile.profile_long: The Valse à deux temps, also known as the Valse Russe, emerged as a significant departure from the standard three-beat waltz in the mid-19th century. Its introduction to France is documented to January 1839, when the Baron de Nieuken, an attaché with the Russian delegation, performed the dance at a ball hosted by Count Mole. The dance challenged the existing musical understanding of the waltz, as it required dancers to execute two distinct movements within the space of a three-beat measure. The first step occurs across the first two beats, while the second step occupies the third beat. This innovation was met with immediate acclaim among the Parisian elite, leading to a decline in the popularity of the traditional three-beat waltz within high-society salons. The dance was characterized by its energy and brio, traits often associated with the Russian dancers of the period. While the elite practiced the precise two-step technique, public ballrooms such as La Chaumière developed a simplified variant, where dancers would jump on alternating feet with less regard for the musical structure. The dance requires a diagonal movement pattern, with partners moving forward and backward while shifting their orientation. Over time, as dancers became more proficient, their movements transitioned from large, primitive steps to more refined, smaller motions. The Valse à deux temps remains a historical example of how international cultural exchange in the 19th century reshaped European ballroom traditions.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in Russia and was introduced to Paris in 1839 by the Baron de Nieuken, who learned the steps from a professor while preparing for a ball given by Count Mole.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers execute a slide to the side on the first beat, bend the knees slightly on the second beat, and bring the trailing foot behind the leading foot on the third beat. The movement is performed on a diagonal path.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is performed to three-beat waltz music, though the dancers interpret the measure as two distinct movements rather than three.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance was performed in 19th-century ballrooms and elite salons, requiring formal attire appropriate for the period.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It served as a social ballroom dance, favored by the Russian delegation and later adopted by Parisian society for its energetic and novel rhythmic interpretation.
sections.notable_figures: The Baron de Nieuken, the Prince of Galitzine, the Count of Damas, and the Marquis de La Baume were among the first practitioners in Paris.
sections.regional_variants: A simplified version was created at the public ballroom La Chaumière, where dancers jumped on alternating feet without strict adherence to the music.
sections.lineage: The dance is a variant of the traditional three-beat waltz.

basic_steps: Slide the left foot to the left on the first beat.
Bend the knees slightly on the second beat.
Bring the right foot quickly behind the left foot on the third beat.
teaching.rhythm: Three-beat measure (3/4 time) interpreted as two movements.
teaching.level_notes: Requires coordination to fit two steps into three beats.

music_profile.sound_description: Standard waltz music in 3/4 time, but interpreted by the dancers as a two-beat rhythm.

movement_profile.footwork: Slide left, bend, step right behind.

signature_moves.name: Two-step sequence
signature_moves.description: Slide on beats 1-2, step behind on beat 3.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Includes slight knee bends; simplified versions include jumps.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid ignoring the diagonal path or failing to coordinate the knee bend with the first two beats.

claims.text: The Valse à deux temps originated in Russia and was introduced to France in the mid-19th century.
claims.quote: Valse à deux temps, waltz à deux temps ("waltz in two beats"), also Valse à deux pas ("waltz of two steps") or Valse Russe ("Russian waltz") ... was a waltz of Russian origin introduced in France in the mid-19th century.

claims.text: The Baron de Nieuken introduced the dance to Paris in 1839 after taking lessons.
claims.quote: In January 1839, the Baron de Nieuken, attaché with the Russian delegation, took dancing lessons with my father, and took them as they were given at the time

claims.text: The dance was performed at a ball hosted by Count Mole.
claims.quote: Our baron had to go one evening to a great ball given by the Count Mole, then Minister of Foreign Affairs, and would have to dance the waltz with some charming Moscow ladies.

claims.text: The dance involves a specific two-step sequence over a three-beat measure.
claims.quote: Right away my father understood that in dance, as in music, two notes can make up a three-beat measure, taking the notes here as movements.

claims.text: A simplified version was practiced at the public ballroom La Chaumière.
claims.quote: the habitués of La Chaumière created a second, simplified kind of two-step waltz, contenting themselves with jumping sometimes on one foot, sometimes on the other

claims.text: The technical execution involves a slide, a knee bend, and a quick step behind.
claims.quote: First beat: Slide the left foot to the left, and stop, bending the knees slightly for the second beat; on the third beat, bring the right foot quickly behind the left one
